transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronan.
Stocks on all three indexes on Wall Street finished Friday
and the week sharply lower as investors took profits
on the artificial intelligence rally rather
than give it new life.
The tech-heavy NASDAQ lost 5.2%.
It has given back all of the year's gains.
The Dow lost 1.9% for the day.
The S&P dropped 3.7%.
The Dow and the S&P are now in correction territory
at 10% below their closing records.
NPR's John Ruich has more on the market sell-off.
>> Many investors have been flip-flopping for months now
between exuberance about the promise of AI
and worries that we're in a bubble.
This week extended a downward slide
that actually started in early October.
AI companies have been pouring billions of dollars into chips,
data centers, and top talent, but it's not clear
that it's all going to pay off in profits for them.
>> The Dow is now below $50,000 for the first time since June.
New data shows a majority of Republicans
in the U.S. don't trust the results
of the midterm elections.
As NPR's Miles Parks reports,
that's despite President Trump himself initially accepting
the results.
>> The new survey data from UC San Diego may be a reality check
for those wondering if Trump's brand of election denial
has run its course in American politics.
Trump, after all, conceded that Republicans
had lost the House and Senate this year.
He blamed the candidates themselves.
Still, just 46% of Republicans
say they felt the midterms were free and fair,
and just 52% said they had confidence
in the country's vote-counting process.
After the 2024 election, which Trump won,
Republican confidence in vote-counting
was 30 percentage points higher.
It is typical for supporters of a losing party
to have some doubts about the process,
but experts say the swings at Republican confidence
in recent years are outside the norm.
Miles Parks, NPR News, Washington.
>> New York City officials released their plan Friday
to close the jail at Rikers Island,
the city's main pretrial detention center.
NPR's Meg Anderson reports the jail has been plagued
with reports of problems for many years.
>> The question of what to do with Rikers
has eluded New York City leaders for years.
Now, New York City Mayor Zoran Mamdani
has pledged to take on the jail's closure head-on.
>> Today, we lead differently.
I am proud that New York City will close Rikers Island
once and for all.
>> The city will build four smaller jails across the city
over the next six years,
which will require a dramatic reduction
in the city's jail population.
The city plan includes more diversion,
more services aimed at crime prevention,
strategies to speed up court cases
and better training and oversight for staff
aimed at not carrying the failures of Rikers
into the new jails.
Meg Anderson, NPR News.
>> And from Washington, you're listening to "NPR News."
In a first-of-its-kind auction,
the Trump administration Friday auctioned deep-sea mining leases
from millions of acres of federal seafloor
near American Samoa in the Pacific Ocean.
Two lease areas were auctioned for the minimum bid
of $3 million.
The leases are subject to numerous lawsuits
by residents of the U.S. territory
and others opposed to the possibility
of the seafloor being mined.
In Atlanta, the death of a 42-year-old educator
who was thrown from the Six Flags
over Georgia roller coaster has been ruled an accident.
From member station WABE, Lily Oppenheimer reports.
>> The Cobb County Medical Examiner's Office
confirmed that Hassan Karim's cause of death
was blunt force injuries and extensive trauma
to his head, neck, and torso.
He was ejected from the Goliath coaster at the Six Flags
just outside of Atlanta last month.
Six Flags has not released results
from an internal investigation into what went wrong that day
but has since added seatbelts to the ride.
Park operators are conducting
a comprehensive safety review of all rides.
Loved ones say Karim was a beloved teacher and father
who worked as an IT manager
at an Atlanta Public Schools Academy.
For NPR News, I'm Lily Oppenheimer in Atlanta.
>> The latest version of Grand Theft Auto 6
is a big hit with gamers.
Rockstar Games, which designed the game,
said the new version generated a record
nearly $3.8 billion in the first day of retail sales,
far exceeding GTA 5,
which made about a billion dollars 13 years ago.
I'm Dan Ronan, NPR News.

New data shows most Republicans don't trust the 2026 midterm election results
New York City unveils plan to close Rikers Island jail and build four smaller jails
Trump administration auctions deep-sea mining leases off American Samoa for minimum bids
Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster death of educator Hassan Karim ruled an accident
Rockstar Games reports Grand Theft Auto 6 earned record $3.8 billion in first day of sales
